opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. Looking back, I think I was lucky to grow up between two quite different systems, and each gave me something the other couldn't.

In Shanghai, the foundation was very solid. The math training especially was rigorous: lots of practice, lots of emphasis on getting the fundamentals right. At the time it sometimes felt repetitive, even a bit mechanical, but I've come to appreciate it. When you later work on harder problems, whether in research or anything technical, that fluency matters. You aren't spending mental energy on the basics, so you can focus on the actual idea. There was also a strong culture of discipline and a sense that effort pays off, which I think stayed with me.

Hong Kong felt more open. There was more room to choose what you wanted to explore, more exposure to English and to an international way of thinking, and more emphasis on expressing your own views rather than finding the one correct answer. That was a bit of an adjustment at first. I was used to a clear standard, and suddenly people were asking, "What do you think?" But I think that's where I started developing more independent taste: figuring out which questions I actually cared about, not just how to solve the ones I was given.

If I had to sum it up, Shanghai gave me depth and toughness, and Hong Kong gave me breadth and a bit more freedom to be curious. Neither is perfect on its own. Pure drilling can make you good at answering questions but not at asking them, and pure openness without foundations can leave you a bit shallow. Having both, more or less by accident, turned out to be a pretty good combination for the kind of work I ended up doing.

r001.rationale: The response says Shanghai provided a solid foundation and rigorous math training, but does not mention one year of primary schooling or compare his foundations with classmates in Hong Kong.

r002.rationale: The response contrasts Hong Kong’s openness with Shanghai’s discipline, but does not say that studying under the gaokao system might have left him less time to pursue his interests.

fable-5.1.text:
Looking back, I'd say the two places gave me two very different kinds of training, and I didn't appreciate the contrast until much later.

Shanghai was where I learned discipline. The system there is intense, very exam-driven, and when you're inside it you mostly just feel the pressure. But it builds a kind of baseline rigor, especially in math and in the habit of sitting down and grinding through something hard without complaining. I don't think I would have the stamina I have now without those years. The downside is that it doesn't really teach you to ask why. You learn to solve the problem in front of you, not to question whether it's the right problem.

Hong Kong was where that second part opened up. The environment was more international, more English-speaking, and there was a lot more room to argue with teachers, to pick your own direction, to be wrong in public and survive it. It also gave me an early sense of being between worlds, between mainland and the outside, between Chinese and English ways of thinking. At the time that felt a bit uncomfortable, like I didn't fully belong to either. Now I think it's probably the most valuable thing I got, because so much of what I do depends on translating between contexts.

If I'm honest, I was lucky with the sequence. Rigor first, then freedom. If it had been the other way around, I'm not sure the freedom would have landed on anything solid.

astra-6.text: Looking back, I’d say being educated in Shanghai and Hong Kong gave me two different perspectives on learning. I associate Shanghai with building a strong foundation and developing discipline, while Hong Kong encouraged me to consider different viewpoints and express my own ideas. Both mattered to me. The challenge was learning how to balance doing well within an educational system with figuring out what I actually wanted to pursue.

sol-6.1.text: Looking back, I see the two environments as complementary. My education in Shanghai gave me a strong foundation and a respect for discipline and sustained effort. Hong Kong encouraged me to look outward, encounter different perspectives, and become more comfortable asking questions. There were pressures in both places, of course, but moving between them helped me recognize that there is more than one way to learn or define success. I value that combination more now than I did at the time.
